stories.headline: Update: Judge Vacates Proud Boys Seditious Conspiracy Convictions, Dismisses Jan. 6 Case With Prejudice
stories.summary:
A federal judge on Friday granted the Justice Department's motion to permanently dismiss the seditious conspiracy case against four Proud Boys members — Ethan Nordean, Joseph Biggs, Zachary Rehl, and Dominic Pezzola — who had been convicted in connection with the January 6, 2021, Capitol riot. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, ruled that the executive branch holds broad constitutional authority over charging decisions and that precedent required granting the government's unopposed motion. The dismissal with prejudice permanently bars the federal government from bringing the same charges against the four men again.

The ruling follows President Trump's earlier commutation of the four men's sentences and a full pardon of former Proud Boys chairman Enrique Tarrio. In April, the Justice Department asked the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals to vacate the convictions; the appeals court granted that request in May, setting the stage for Friday's final dismissal.

Judge Kelly was careful to note that granting the motion did not constitute the court's endorsement of the administration's approach to January 6 prosecutions. In his seven-page opinion, he wrote that 'no one should mistake the Court's granting the Government's motion for its agreement with those decisions,' and devoted a final section to describing January 6 as an attack on the constitutional process of peaceful transfer of power.

Critics, including many Democrats and some legal scholars, have condemned the administration's systematic unwinding of January 6 prosecutions as an abuse of executive power and a threat to the rule of law. Supporters of the administration argue that the prosecutions were politically motivated overreach and that the president acted within his constitutional pardon authority.

stories.headline: Update: Graham Platner Formally Withdraws from Maine Senate Race; Democrats Scramble to Replace Him
stories.summary:
Democratic Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner officially filed paperwork Friday with the state's Secretary of State withdrawing his candidacy, confirming his exit from the race following sexual assault allegations he denies. The filing — submitted ahead of a Monday deadline — triggers a process in which the Maine Democratic Party must select a replacement candidate by July 27, with a nominating convention planned in Bangor. At least eight Democrats have already entered the field to replace Platner on the November ballot.

The Maine race is considered critical to Democrats' effort to recapture a Senate majority, and Platner's collapse — after a campaign already shadowed by the revelation of a Nazi tattoo — has left the party in disarray with fewer than four months until the midterms. Independent political analysts, including Larry Sabato of the University of Virginia, noted that Maine was expected to be an easy Democratic pickup but is now 'turning out to be tough,' while races in Ohio, Iowa, and Alaska have grown more competitive.

The new development today is Platner's formal, legal withdrawal filing — moving beyond his Wednesday public announcement and officially opening the door for the party to seat a new nominee. Candidates who have entered the race include figures backed by progressive and moderate wings of the party, with divisions already apparent; Senator Tammy Duckworth has publicly opposed one contender, Nirav Shah, over his handling of a deadly Legionnaires' disease outbreak in Illinois.

The scramble reflects broader tensions within the Democratic Party between its progressive and working-class wings. Some Platner backers, particularly women in Maine, have expressed grief over the loss of his candidacy despite the allegations, while national party leaders are pressing for a candidate capable of appealing to rural and independent voters in the state.

stories.headline: Murder Arrest Made After Body of Former British Minister Ann Widdecombe Found at Devon Home
stories.summary:
British police arrested a 26-year-old man Friday on suspicion of murdering Ann Widdecombe, a former Conservative cabinet minister and prominent Reform UK politician, whose body was discovered Thursday morning at her home in Haytor, Devon, with a head injury. The suspect was detained at an address in Newton Abbot, near the scene of the death. Widdecombe was a longtime fixture of British political life, having served as a minister under John Major and later becoming a high-profile Brexit campaigner and Reform UK figure.

Authorities have not disclosed a motive, and the investigation remains in its early stages. The arrest marks a concrete new development following Thursday's discovery of her body. Widdecombe was widely known for her outspoken conservative views on immigration, capital punishment, and social policy, and her death drew immediate reactions from across the British political spectrum.

The case has drawn significant attention in the United Kingdom given Widdecombe's public profile and the violent circumstances of her death. Further details about the suspect's identity or any connection to the victim have not been released by police.

stories.headline: Apple Sues OpenAI for Trade Secret Theft
stories.summary:
Apple filed a civil lawsuit Friday in federal court in the Northern District of California accusing OpenAI and two former Apple employees of systematically stealing the company's trade secrets. The complaint alleges OpenAI exploited job interview processes to extract confidential information about Apple's tools, unreleased products, and internal processes, with the iPhone maker accusing the AI firm of attempting to "free-ride off Apple's decades of innovation."

The lawsuit names OpenAI and two individuals accused of taking Apple's confidential information and transferring it to the competitor. The legal action comes amid a broader talent exodus from Apple to OpenAI, as the frontier AI lab prepares to launch its first hardware device. Apple and OpenAI had struck a partnership in 2024 to integrate AI services into Apple devices, but relations between the companies have since deteriorated.

The case is among the highest-profile corporate intellectual property disputes in the AI industry to date, pitting two of the most valuable technology companies against each other. It also raises broader questions about the competitive dynamics of the AI race, where rapid talent movement between firms has made trade secret protection increasingly difficult to enforce.

The lawsuit was covered by five outlets spanning center and right-leaning publications, reflecting its significance across the technology and business landscape. OpenAI has not yet issued a formal public response to the complaint.

stories.headline: Ryanair Passenger Nearly Sucked Out of Plane Window Over Greece After Mid-Air Decompression
stories.summary:
A Ryanair flight from Thessaloniki, Greece, to Memmingen, Germany, made an emergency return Friday after a cabin window dislodged mid-air approximately ten minutes after takeoff, causing rapid decompression. Passengers reported that a 61-year-old Serbian man was pulled head and shoulders out of the opening before fellow passengers and his wife held onto his legs for roughly five minutes to prevent him from being ejected from the aircraft.

The plane descended approximately 9,000 feet before landing safely back in Thessaloniki. Oxygen masks deployed, and passengers described hearing what sounded like an explosion and being unable to breathe during the incident. The injured man, treated at a Greek hospital for friction burns, was described as conscious but in shock. Ryanair confirmed the window dislodged and said the aircraft landed normally, with a replacement plane later ferrying passengers to their destination.

Passengers told local media that shards from the jet's engine may have struck and broken the window, though Ryanair has not confirmed that account. The aircraft involved was an 18-year-old plane operated by Ryanair's subsidiary Malta Air. Greek aviation authorities and the Hellenic Air and Rail Safety Investigation Authority have opened an investigation.

The incident raises immediate questions about aircraft maintenance standards, particularly for aging planes in budget airline fleets. The Irish Aviation Authority said it was monitoring the situation and would assist investigators as needed.

stories.headline: Cyclospora Parasite Outbreak Surges; Michigan Reports Over 1,500 Cases, Dozens of States Investigating
stories.summary:
A foodborne parasitic outbreak caused by cyclospora cayetanensis has expanded significantly, with Michigan now reporting more than 1,500 confirmed cases as of July 10 and neighboring Ohio logging hundreds more. Health officials say active investigations are underway in more than two dozen other states, though no specific food source has been identified as the origin of the outbreak.

Cyclosporiasis is an intestinal illness transmitted through food or water contaminated with fecal matter. While not fatal, the infection can cause severe and prolonged gastrointestinal symptoms, including explosive diarrhea lasting from days to more than a month, along with nausea, fatigue, and bloating. The illness can be treated with antibiotics, though many recover without medical intervention over a longer period.

Investigators face an unusually difficult task in tracing the source because the parasite cannot be reproduced in a laboratory setting, and many standard food poisoning tests do not detect it. The investigation is further complicated by a 2025 CDC decision to make state reporting of cyclospora optional after scaling back its Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network, limiting the agency's visibility into case trends nationwide.

Health officials are urging residents and restaurants in outbreak hotspots to follow strict food safety protocols, including cooking vegetables to at least 158 degrees Fahrenheit — the temperature at which cyclospora is destroyed. Officials note that direct person-to-person transmission is unlikely, and that careful food handling remains the primary preventive measure until a source is identified.

stories.headline: Update: U.S.-Iran Conflict Continues as Strikes Expand Across Region; Ceasefire in Doubt
stories.summary:
The United States launched fresh airstrikes against Iran, hitting approximately 90 targets including airport runways and missile launchers, while Iran responded by targeting U.S.-allied Gulf states including Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar. Sirens sounded multiple times in Bahrain, home to the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet headquarters, marking a significant escalation in the geographic scope of the conflict. The exchange threatens an interim ceasefire agreement that was already under severe strain.

President Trump declared the ceasefire "over" via Truth Social while simultaneously agreeing to allow diplomatic talks to continue, a contradictory posture that has left the status of negotiations unclear. Iranian officials have not formally called off the interim peace agreement, and American officials confirmed back-channel discussions remain active. Neither side appears ready to return to formal talks, and Iran has not committed to restoring free passage through the Strait of Hormuz.

The conflict's expansion into Gulf states marks a new threshold, drawing in U.S. regional allies who host major American military installations and represent critical nodes in global oil infrastructure. The IMF has already cut its global growth forecast citing the energy shock from the war. Diplomatic efforts by regional mediators are continuing, but analysts warn that back-to-back days of strikes have pushed the situation toward potential full-scale military conflict.

Unidentified airstrikes also hit Iran after the U.S. declared its own strikes complete, raising questions about whether Israel or another party may be conducting parallel operations. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a significant share of global oil passes, remains a flashpoint. Trump's public and private messaging continues to diverge, complicating efforts to read U.S. intentions in the region.

stories.headline: Democratic Operatives Placed Copycat Candidate on Alaska Senate Ballot to Confuse Voters, Elections Officials Find
stories.summary:
Alaska's Division of Elections has found that a candidate named Dan Sullivan entered the state's Senate race with the apparent intent to confuse voters who intended to cast ballots for Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan of the same name. The finding implicates Democratic operatives in a deliberate ballot-spoiling scheme targeting one of the most closely watched Senate races of the 2026 midterm cycle. The story has drawn coverage from 21 outlets across the political spectrum.

The tactic, known as a "copycat" or "sham" candidacy, is designed to siphon votes from a target candidate by exploiting name recognition on the ballot. Republicans have characterized the move as election manipulation and a threat to electoral integrity, calling for accountability for those behind the effort. Democrats have not publicly claimed responsibility for organizing the candidate's filing.

The revelation comes amid an already turbulent midterm election environment, with the Trump administration separately firing the three remaining members of the Election Assistance Commission — the sole federal agency dedicated to election administration — just months before November voting. Critics including former Obama strategist David Axelrod warned that the EAC dismissals, combined with the Alaska ballot scheme, represent compounding threats to election fairness from different directions.

The Alaska case is distinct from the EAC firings but together they illustrate the degree to which election administration and electoral integrity have become active battlegrounds ahead of the midterms. The Alaska Division of Elections has not yet announced what, if any, remedies are available given filing deadlines. Legal challenges are expected.

stories.headline: Trump Fires All Three Election Assistance Commission Members Ahead of Midterms
stories.summary:
President Trump ousted all three remaining members of the bipartisan U.S. Election Assistance Commission on Thursday, leaving the agency without leadership less than four months before the November midterm elections. Democratic commissioners Thomas Hicks and Benjamin Hovland were terminated by email, while Republican commissioner Christy McCormick received a phone call and was asked to resign. A White House official confirmed all three are gone and said replacements are forthcoming, though presidential appointments to the EAC require Senate confirmation — a process that could take months.

The EAC is a federally mandated bipartisan body that helps state and local officials administer elections, certifies voting equipment, and has distributed more than $1 billion in election security grants since 2018. Critics say gutting the commission on the eve of midterms will leave election administrators without a key federal resource. Former commissioner Hovland warned of a "death-by-1,000-cuts" scenario in which understaffed election offices become more prone to errors.

Administration critics, including Arizona Democratic Secretary of State Adrian Fontes, called the move "irresponsible and dangerous" and said it undermines nonpartisan election administration. Democrats framed the firings as part of a broader effort to weaken election oversight infrastructure. The White House has not publicly stated its rationale beyond confirming the dismissals and promising replacements. The EAC had already been operating with three members instead of its normal four after a Republican commissioner resigned earlier this year.

stories.headline: Spain Wildfire Kills at Least 12, More Than 20 Still Missing in Andalusia
stories.summary:
A wildfire in southern Spain's Andalusia region has killed at least 12 people and left more than 20 others missing, making it one of the deadliest blazes on record in the country. Spanish authorities said many of the victims were foreign tourists. The cause of the fire has not been determined.

The blaze struck amid an intense heat wave that has pushed temperatures in southern Spain to nearly 106 degrees Fahrenheit. Spain is among several European nations battered by extreme heat this summer, conditions that dramatically increase wildfire risk and spread. Emergency crews were still working the scene Friday.

The death toll and number of missing persons make this a significant life-safety event with regional and tourism implications across one of Europe's most-visited areas. Authorities have not yet announced evacuation figures or estimated the total area burned.

stories.headline: Trump Refuses to Sign Bipartisan Housing Bill in Protest Over Senate's Failure to Pass Voter ID Legislation
stories.summary:
President Trump announced Friday he will not sign the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a landmark bipartisan housing bill that cleared Congress, as a symbolic protest against the Senate's failure to pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, which would tighten voter identification requirements. Trump posted that the SAVE Act's non-passage was "CRAZY" and a threat to any politician who voted against it. Despite his refusal to sign, the White House confirmed Trump does not intend to veto the bill either.

Because the president has 10 days to act on legislation and he is not exercising a veto, the housing bill is set to become law automatically at midnight Friday. The episode is therefore largely symbolic — the housing legislation will take effect regardless — but it underscores the ongoing tension between Trump and Senate Republicans over voting-restriction priorities.

Supporters of the housing bill, which had broad bipartisan backing, expressed frustration that the legislation's passage was being overshadowed by intra-Republican friction over voter ID. Critics of the SAVE Act, primarily Democrats, argue existing laws already prohibit noncitizens from voting and that the bill is designed to suppress legitimate voters. Proponents say it closes a gap in federal verification requirements. The episode illustrates continuing divisions within the Republican coalition even as Trump seeks to exercise leverage over his own party's legislators.

stories.headline: Andy Burnham Secures Near-Certain Path to UK Prime Minister After Labour MPs Back Him Overwhelmingly
stories.summary:
Andy Burnham has emerged as the near-certain next leader of the UK Labour Party and prime minister after 322 of 403 Labour Members of Parliament nominated him on the first day of the party's leadership contest to replace Keir Starmer. The lopsided vote effectively settles the contest before it formally concludes, putting Burnham — the current Mayor of Greater Manchester — on track to lead Britain's government.

Burnham said he was 'deeply grateful' for the support from his parliamentary colleagues, describing it as reflecting 'a shared belief that Britain needs' a new direction. The leadership race was triggered by Starmer's departure, though details of that exit were not specified in the coverage.

The outcome carries significant implications for British domestic and foreign policy, including the UK's relationships with the European Union, NATO allies, and the United States at a moment of heightened geopolitical tension over the Iran conflict and the ongoing war in Ukraine. Burnham is broadly associated with the left-leaning wing of the Labour Party and has emphasized northern English economic renewal as a signature theme.

stories.headline: Qatar Investment Authority Vetoes Volkswagen-Rafael Defense Joint Venture, Threatening Hundreds of German Jobs
stories.summary:
The Qatar Investment Authority has blocked a planned cooperation between German automaker Volkswagen and Israeli defense company Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, according to people familiar with the matter. The joint venture had been structured in part to preserve hundreds of jobs at one of Volkswagen's manufacturing sites.

Qatar, which holds a significant stake in Volkswagen through its sovereign wealth fund, exercised its veto in what amounts to a direct intervention by a Gulf state in a European industrial partnership with an Israeli firm. The move reflects the broader economic and diplomatic pressure on Western companies with ties to Israel amid the ongoing conflict in Gaza and the wider regional war.

The decision places Volkswagen in a difficult position, as it must now find alternative arrangements to secure the jobs that the Rafael partnership was intended to protect. The episode illustrates the growing complexity facing European corporations navigating relationships with both Gulf sovereign investors and Israeli defense partners simultaneously.

stories.headline: Medicare Launches Pilot Program Offering Weight Loss Drugs at $50 a Month for Millions of Beneficiaries
stories.summary:
Starting this month, some Medicare beneficiaries can purchase GLP-1 weight loss drugs for $50 per month under a new temporary government pilot program, a steep discount from retail prices that can reach hundreds of dollars monthly. The Bridge Program is scheduled to run through the end of 2027 and is designed to reach Medicare enrollees who cannot access GLP-1 coverage through their Part D prescription drug plans, which are legally prohibited from covering drugs used solely for weight loss.

According to analysis by KFF, approximately four million Medicare beneficiaries meet the clinical and eligibility criteria for the program. To qualify, a patient must have a body mass index over 35, or a BMI over 27 combined with conditions such as prediabetes or hypertension — but must not already have type 2 diabetes, sleep apnea, or fatty liver disease, conditions for which GLP-1 coverage is already available under Part D.

The program comes as GLP-1 drug use surges across the United States. A new Gallup poll finds 11 percent of American adults currently use one of the medications, up sharply from 3 percent two years ago. The fiscal implications for Medicare are substantial, as the government will shoulder a significant portion of the drug costs for a potentially large and growing beneficiary population.

stories.headline: Greek F-16 Crash-Lands at Zakynthos Airport, Closing Runway During Peak Summer Season
stories.summary:
A Hellenic Air Force F-16 fighter jet made an emergency crash-landing at Zakynthos International Airport in Greece on Thursday after developing a technical fault mid-flight, closing one of the country's busiest summer holiday terminals. The aircraft, which was on a training flight from the 335 Squadron based at Araxos Air Base, landed at approximately 1:45 p.m. local time without deploying its landing gear and slid dozens of meters along the runway before catching fire.

Firefighters and airport emergency personnel responded immediately and doused the blaze. The Hellenic Air Force confirmed the pilot was in good health and that an investigation into the cause has been launched, though it did not comment on reports that the pilot received an onboard fire warning before landing.

The runway closure caused widespread delays, with all remaining Thursday flights pushed back to 9 p.m. local time or later. Zakynthos is a major destination for British and European tourists during the summer season, with thousands of visitors transiting the airport weekly. A specialist air force team was dispatched to remove the aircraft and restore normal airport operations.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Strikes 90 More Iranian Targets as Conflict Escalates; Khamenei Buried in Mashhad
stories.summary:
U.S. Central Command conducted strikes on 90 Iranian targets in the latest round of attacks, with Iran's health ministry reporting 14 people killed since Tuesday. The strikes represent the most intense exchange between the two countries since the ceasefire was declared over by President Trump, and officials describe this week as the worst period of hostilities since that breakdown.

Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who died in earlier U.S. and Israeli airstrikes, was buried Friday in his hometown of Mashhad following days of public mourning and large funeral processions across Iran. Khamenei ruled Iran for nearly 37 years and is only the second ruler of the nation to be interred in Mashhad. Crowds carried Iranian flags and signs calling for the deaths of Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu.

President Trump also spoke with Netanyahu about U.S. 'moves' in the Persian Gulf, according to the Associated Press, as financial markets remained on edge over the conflict's trajectory. Oil prices eased somewhat Thursday as markets paused to assess the situation, though the IMF has already cut global growth forecasts citing the Iran war's energy shock.

Supporters of Khamenei view him as a martyr who defied Western pressure, while large sectors of Iranian society remain deeply disillusioned after decades of crackdowns, economic stagnation, and the January crackdown that killed thousands. The ongoing conflict has complicated a U.S.-brokered Lebanon-Israel deal and raised fears of renewed Hezbollah fighting.

stories.headline: Typhoon Bavi Kills 15 in Philippines Landslides, Threatens Taiwan and China
stories.summary:
Typhoon Bavi, described as one of the strongest storms in decades and spanning roughly 1,000 kilometers at its widest point, has killed at least 15 people through landslides on the Philippine island of Mindanao, with rescuers still searching for the missing. The storm is now sweeping across the Pacific toward Taiwan, where authorities have warned of up to one meter of rainfall and placed 29,000 soldiers on standby.

Taiwanese officials say Bavi could be the largest storm by size to hit the island since 1987. Dozens of flights have been cancelled across the region, supermarket shelves have been cleared by residents stocking up on supplies, and farmers rushed to protect crops before the storm's arrival. Japan Airlines and All Nippon Airways have collectively cancelled more than 260 flights, disrupting roughly 40,000 passengers.

After Taiwan, the typhoon is expected to make landfall in southeastern China's Fujian province, with forecasts suggesting it could strike China twice as it moves northward. Northern Chinese provinces, which have less experience with major typhoons than the south, have been urged to strengthen preparations. Parts of southern China are already recovering from the devastation of Typhoon Maysak, which struck earlier.

stories.headline: Suspected Ebola Patients Quarantined in Same Hotel as U.S. Deportees in Equatorial Guinea
stories.summary:
Migrants deported from the United States and held in a hotel in Equatorial Guinea say authorities have used the same facility to quarantine at least two suspected Ebola patients, according to deportees and their lawyers. Medical personnel in hazmat suits were seen transporting the patients to the hotel, which houses 17 deportees from countries including Angola, Mauritania, and Ethiopia under a third-country deportation deal with the Trump administration.

The hotel, located on a tropical island off Equatorial Guinea's coast and owned by President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, also served as an isolation center during the Covid-19 pandemic. Deportees said they were informed by a doctor that the individuals were suspected Ebola cases and told to be careful, but were provided no masks, disinfectants, or other protective supplies, and received no formal briefing on risk-reduction measures.

Equatorial Guinea shares no border with the Democratic Republic of Congo, where a rare Ebola strain has killed over 600 people since May, and no confirmed cases have been reported in Equatorial Guinea. However, a coalition of international lawyers called the situation alarming and said they had received reports from multiple detained individuals corroborating the account. One detainee described deteriorating conditions, saying hygiene was 'unimaginable' and that no one was communicating with them about their status or safety.

stories.headline: China Successfully Lands Reusable Rocket for First Time, Challenging U.S. Space Dominance
stories.summary:
China successfully recovered a reusable rocket booster for the first time Friday, when the Long March 10B lifted off from Hainan province and its booster returned to Earth vertically approximately six minutes after stage separation, landing on a floating platform at sea. The achievement marks a significant milestone for China's space program and signals a potential challenge to the reusable rocket dominance held by SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Blue Origin's New Glenn.

The Long March 10B, capable of carrying at least 16 metric tons to low-Earth orbit, is comparable in capacity to SpaceX's Falcon 9. Unlike the Falcon 9, which lands autonomously on ground pads or drone ships, the Chinese rocket uses 'landing hooks' that catch a net attached to a floating platform. China had made a first attempt at recovery in February with the Long March 10A, which completed a controlled descent but splashed down next to rather than on the recovery platform.

Reusable rockets significantly reduce the cost of satellite launches and space exploration by allowing the most expensive component — the booster — to be recovered and reflown. SpaceX's Falcon 9 now launches roughly 150 times per year using boosters capable of dozens of reuses. Shares in Chinese space companies rose 10 percent, the daily limit permitted under Chinese financial market rules, following Friday's announcement.
